claims.text: The primary source is an Intercontinental Exchange release dated 2026-10-29: a definitive agreement with Trade[XYZ] under which ICE becomes "the exclusive operator" of Trade[XYZ]'s regulated markets
The release names no regulator and no registration category, gives no launch date, and says customers would be KYC/AML-verified and reach the venue through futures commission merchants.
Trade[XYZ] is not Hyperliquid. It is a builder that deploys markets under Hyperliquid's HIP-3 framework
HIP-3 deployers must keep 500,000 HYPE staked.
{date: 2026-05-29, headline: "CFTC approves Kalshi BTCPERP", body: "First true perpetual approved as a futures contract under Reg. 40.3."}
{date: 2026-10-30, headline: "Wilson's five questions", body: "Posted 14:44 UTC; 88,920 views at fetch."}
On 2026-10-30 Don Wilson, founder of DRW and Cumberland, thanked the CFTC chairman for "experimentation"
Bankless identified Price on 2026-06-02 as "a DeFi investor and Lighter advisor" who argued LIT was underpriced.
five months before the deal, ICE and CME were reported pressing regulators about Hyperliquid, citing "insider trading and price manipulation risks."
Price writes that Lighter's matching engine is centralized and that speed is not traded against security.
Lighter's own documentation confirms price-time priority with sequencer-provided FIFO ordering and "soft finality."
latency improves linearly from 0 to 8 basis points, at roughly 45 ms per basis point, and higher rates only break ties inside a 70 ms bucket.
Passive orders pay a rate on resting notional, sorted within a 400 ms window, and the fee is charged whether or not the order fills.
Cancels always go ahead of executable orders, and the fees are burned rather than paid to validators.

Gossip priority is a separate Dutch auction, re-run every three minutes, that buys about 25 ms of earlier read access per slot, resetting to ten times the prior winning price with a floor of 0.1 HYPE.
A secondary report counts $3.16M collected since the 2026-04-13 launch, roughly split between the two mechanisms (that figure is not independently verified).
The docs page restricts order priority only to orders on a "non-outcome asset"; secondary reports describe it as limited to HIP-3 markets, and we could not reconcile the two.
Standard accounts pay 0% maker and 0% taker but carry a 300 ms delay on takers and on cancel or modify requests; makers carry none.
The opt-in Premium account cuts taker latency to 140 ms for 0.0280% (2.8 bp) taker and 0.0040% maker fees, discounted up to 30% by staking 500,000 LIT.
One critic estimated the "free" tier costs 6 to 12 bp in adverse selection, but that is opinion with no data behind it, and the premium latency numbers he cited have since changed.
The statutory core principles for designated contract markets do not mention paid priority or latency access.
Regulation 38.151 requires access criteria that are "impartial, transparent, and applied in a non-discriminatory manner" and "comparable fee structures" for equal access.
Core Principle 9 requires "a competitive, open, and efficient market and mechanism for executing transactions."
Core Principle 12 requires rules "to promote fair and equitable trading."[^21] Core Principle 7 requires the execution mechanism itself to be published.
The CFTC itself may not publish data that would "separately disclose the business transactions or market positions of any person," and large-trader reports flow to it daily
No rule we retrieved requires a public order book, and the rulebook standard is publication of the rules and mechanisms, not of positions.
a foreign board of trade cannot permit direct access to its matching system from the US without registration under Part 48.
staff Letter 26-17 allows Coinbase's futures commission merchant to offer offshore perps as foreign futures and accept digital commodities or stablecoins as margin at a foreign affiliate.

The agency also approved Kalshi's BTCPERP on 2026-05-29 under Regulation 40.3, found it consistent with the core principles, noted the design "may not be suitable for all asset classes," and invited other perpetual submissions.
L2BEAT's independent analysis, dated 2026-05-22, found the mechanism sound: if the operator stops processing a forced priority transaction for 14 days
L2BEAT rebuilt the verifier bytecode "byte-for-byte" and reproduced the state root from blobs alone across about 5,000 batches.
Open positions "cash-settle at the last published mark price," and live orders and matching-engine state are lost.

L2BEAT rates Lighter Stage 0, lists three permissioned operator addresses, and shows that regular upgrades have a 21-day delay but that a 4-of-7 Security Council can reduce it to zero, which L2BEAT flags as critical; 91 upgrades had occurred at fetch time.
A forced order via the L1 queue is limited to reduce-only IOC orders, withdrawals and share burns, and the L1 messaging contract was scheduled to change on 2026-11-08.

An independent audit of the block circuits by zkSecurity found two high-severity bugs, one of which would let a malicious prover create an account with arbitrary collateral; all but one finding were fixed.
Hyperliquid positions are queryable by address with no authentication.
During the 2025-10-10 crash, more than $19B was wiped out in total, $10.08B of it on Hyperliquid, with over 6,300 wallets liquidated and auto-deleveraging firing for the first time.
The JELLY episode cost the vault about $12M at peak by one count, while other outlets report $4M or $10M-plus, and validators force-settled the market.
A market-maker infrastructure founder relayed that a top Hyperliquid maker rotates strategies every three weeks because they get copied
posts encrypted blobs under a symmetric key itself encrypted to a three-member council; L2BEAT records that any one member can decrypt and that "there is no generic escape hatch mechanism."
StarkEx's perpetual exit shows the other side of the coupling: the withdrawable amount is computed from the vault's position and the prices of all assets in the last batch
Lighter posts per-account state differences as blobs, not per-trade records; placing and cancelling orders are proven but not posted.
Blob fees fell structurally after the Fusaka upgrade and subsequent blob-parameter-only forks raised capacity, though Fusaka also added an execution-linked fee floor.
A replay of mid-2026 blob prices found a median around 0.005 gwei per blob gas, but that statistic comes from a secondary summary and we found no October 2026 figure.

An L2BEAT-derived summary put Lighter's total Ethereum settlement cost at about $306K over twelve months, roughly $839 a day; against reported annual revenue of about $45M that is under 1%, though both numbers are secondary.
Ethereum-block proving cost on the Ethproofs benchmark fell from $1.69 to under $0.04 during 2025 by one report
L2BEAT records average intervals of about 3m40s for batch submission, 3m41s for proofs and 6m53s for state updates, with a stall of more than four hours on 2026-10-29.
Until a proof lands, a trade is "soft-final" on the sequencer's word.
Secondary reports citing DefiLlama put thirty-day perp volume on 2026-10-15 at roughly $209.5B for Hyperliquid and $62.7B for Lighter, with open interest of $7.70B against $711M.
The shares are ARA arithmetic on the snapshot's venue volumes over its stated $597.8B total.
A 21Shares note in October 2025 flagged a volume-to-TVL ratio above 70:1 against a healthy 3 to 7 and raised "possible wash trading"
After its token launched on 2025-12-30, reports describe daily volume falling from $7-12B to about $2-4B.
Sector volume fell more than 50% from the October 2025 peak.
The 2025-10-10 crash also knocked Lighter offline for about 4.5 hours after a database failure, with over 2,000 affected users and a liquidity-pool loss.
Lighter's late-2025 lead coincided with a zero-fee points programme.
Wilson's own proposed remedy in his May op-ed was privacy and limited pre-trade visibility, not abandoning chains.
Wilson's post refers to "@NYSE working to bring @HyperliquidX onshore."
